coaching.overall_assessment: The 23.51-second climb shows an economy of upper-body effort characterized by low cumulative time spent in deep arm flexion (1.10s total on the left arm and 0.45s on the right arm). Vertical hip velocity fluctuates between downward preparatory dips (notably at 15.19s) and strong upward propulsion phases (peaking at 17.52s and 22.19s), indicating periodic dynamic progression rather than continuous static climbing.
strengths: Efficient arm extension: The low total duration of deep bends (left: 1.10s, right: 0.45s) and short average durations (0.14s left, 0.06s right) suggest the climber frequently maintains straighter arm positions rather than over-relying on sustained static lock-offs.

Lower-body power generation: At 15.19s, the left knee achieves deep flexion (66.36°), which directly precedes the climb's highest upward hip velocity (+0.108 at 17.52s), indicating effective force transmission from the lower body.
Quick movement execution: When deep arm bends occur, they are generally resolved quickly (longest continuous deep bend is 0.65s at 22.38s), indicating fast target acquisition on holds.
improvements: Minimize downward hip sagging: Pronounced negative vertical hip velocities at 4.67s (-0.044), 10.51s (-0.048), 15.19s (-0.121), and 19.86s (-0.053) suggest instances of sagging or loss of body tension; focusing on core engagement and high foot placement before initiating reaches can smooth out vertical progression.

Reduce movement hesitation: Multiple deep bend intervals on the left arm were logged as 'interrupted' early in the route (at 0.67s, 0.93s, and 3.00s), which may reflect readjustments, regripping, or indecision during movement initiation.

Evaluate sustained right-arm flexion in the upper section: Between 16.35s and 19.86s, the right elbow angle remains moderately flexed between 94.5° and 107.5°; assessing whether foot placement allows this arm to fully extend could help preserve upper-body stamina.
limitations: Tracking occlusions: Frequent null values exist for the left elbow (e.g., 1.17s, 3.50s, 4.67s–7.01s) and the right knee (15.19s–19.86s), likely caused by limb self-occlusion or body rotation relative to the camera.

Lack of 3D spatial and route context: MediaPipe data provides planar joint angles and velocities without contextual metrics such as wall angle, hold size/type, body proximity to the wall, or center-of-mass shift along the z-axis.
Sample resolution: The movement samples are spaced at ~1.17-second intervals, meaning fast micro-adjustments and peak forces between samples are not captured.
